extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate geoscience students and their instructors (geology educators teaching research/proposal writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing undergraduate-level geoscience research proposals and for teaching hypothesis testing in the geosciences; emphasizes formulation of testable hypotheses, multiple working hypotheses, methods for testing, and convincing arguments of feasibility and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional proposal organization (four parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A traditional proposal has four parts: (1) a statement of the hypothesis or hypotheses, (2) arguments that the hypotheses merit testing, (3) explanation of proposed tests, and (4) demonstration that you can successfully complete the tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this structure to organize the proposal; the proposal explains the nuts and bolts of the research and positions it within pressing problems and questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior work and identify outstanding questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, consider what has already been done and what could be done: what have others accomplished, what outstanding questions or problems remain, which techniques or field areas show promise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search literature (including authors' 'future work' suggestions), identify tractable questions, and do not be afraid to think small—many projects progress by incremental steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate testable hypotheses (and distinguish from questions/goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the transition from questions to testable hypotheses. A hypothesis is a proposition phrased so that it could be proven true or false; it is not a question or a research goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorm many hypotheses, then choose two or a few interesting hypotheses that you could realistically test. Beware the common flaw of an interesting hypothesis that is exceedingly difficult to test; balance interest with feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple working hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop multiple hypotheses in the early stages rather than focusing on a single hypothesis, to avoid bias and premature attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Chamberlin's admonition to bring every rational explanation into view and give each an impartial working form; be the 'parent of a family of hypotheses' and avoid fastening affection on one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification / elimination as a selection strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Select among hypotheses by elimination (falsification): show that some hypotheses are incapable of producing the observed phenomena and discard the 'weaklings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gilbert's example demonstrates using calculations/models to eliminate hypotheses; recognize that hypotheses are rarely proved true absolutely, so falsification is a practical way to narrow options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modeling and quantitative analysis to test feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple calculations or models to determine which hypotheses are physically possible given quantitative knowledge of processes and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling can strengthen a surviving hypothesis by showing it could produce observed magnitudes/behaviors; models help explore what is possible even if they are not final tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek smoking guns (positive, discriminating field evidence) for historical hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: For historical/geologic causal hypotheses, look for positive evidence — 'smoking guns' — that pick out one competing hypothesis as a better causal explanation for available traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleland emphasizes that field data often provide smoking guns (e.g., iridium anomaly for meteorite impact). While lab work and models suggest what to look for, only field traces can serve as definitive discriminating evidence for historical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prediction / 'unlike consequences' to discriminate hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce consequences peculiar to each hypothesis (predictions) and gather data that will allow discrimination between competing hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson's approach: analyze each hypothesis to determine what characteristic observations it predicts; these 'unlike consequences' have high critical value in discriminating valid vs invalid hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain exactly how proposed data/methods/tests will test hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the research you will do to test hypotheses: what data (field, lab), models, or experiments you will use; what variables and knowledge will be incorporated; and precisely how these would test the hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether you propose to confirm or falsify hypotheses, list specific predictions, indicate whether you're seeking a smoking gun, and describe step-by-step how data/models/experiments discriminate among hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate feasibility and capability to complete tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that you can successfully carry out the proposed tests (resources, methods, locations, materials, lab access, modeling capability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposal must convince the reviewer that you can do the research: explain logistics, skills, time scale, and why your approach is practicable given constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate scale for hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Find an appropriate scale for hypotheses—between grand, nearly untestable questions and trivial specifics; most scientific research occurs in small steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proposing to test hypotheses that are too ambitious (e.g., origin of Great Lakes) or too trivial; choose questions that match available data and realistic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about relationships among multiple hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing multiple working hypotheses, explain how they relate: are they compatible or mutually exclusive, and would confirmation/falsification of one affect the others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear the logical relationships among hypotheses so reviewers understand how tests inform the broader set of explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate hypotheses clearly and early, then flesh them out
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate your hypotheses as clearly and quickly as possible at the start of the proposal, then expand on them with context, justification, and testing strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear concise statement upfront helps orient the reader; subsequent sections should elaborate links to literature, plausibility, and detailed methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position research in context and argue its significance and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arguments (not just literature summary) to establish that your hypotheses are plausible and worth testing, and explain why the hypotheses interest geologists or other constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond citing prior work, state how your research addresses pressing problems, fills gaps, or advances understanding; reviewers need to be convinced of intellectual merit and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with assumptions and analyze constituent parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform analysis by separating observations, arguments, and conclusions into constituent parts, tracing each part back to its source and testing its validity; be careful with your assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson's 'analysis' warns that assumptions underlying discriminatory tests may be invalid; scrutinize assumptions and validate auxiliary premises that enable predictions or inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize complexity and iterative/circular reasoning in geoscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that geoscientific reasoning is often non-linear and involves iterative back-and-forth between data at different scales; circular reasoning is common and can be productive if properly handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frodeman describes reasoning where interpretations at one level inform and are informed by other levels; acknowledge this complexity and use iterative tests, but avoid uncritical circularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose discriminating observations (highest critical value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on observations or data that most effectively discriminate among hypotheses — those with the highest critical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tests that yield unlike consequences; prioritize gathering data that will most directly rule in or out competing explanations rather than ambiguous or equivocal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recent primary literature as springboards for proposal topics
rubrics_metrics.description: For teaching and student proposals, use recent research papers (e.g., Science, Nature) as starting points: students present papers and can use them to generate novel, tractable proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach brings cutting-edge research into the classroom, encourages choice and student interest, and helps students learn to move from published results to next-step hypotheses and tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common anti-patterns: single-hypothesis bias, untestable aims, and overreliance on textbook controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Common flaws include focusing on a single hypothesis (leading to bias), developing hypotheses that are exceedingly difficult to test, and writing proposals that merely repeat textbook-stalled debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly counter these by using multiple hypotheses, selecting testable and appropriately scaled questions, and grounding proposals in current literature and realistic methods.
